processing: As with other Wuyi rock teas: withered, shaken, partly oxidised, rolled and then roasted. Roast level varies by maker.
harvest_season: Little is documented for this cultivar; Wuyi rock teas are normally picked once a year in spring.
appearance_dry: Typical of Wuyi rock teas: long, twisted dark strips with a brownish sheen.
appearance_liquor: Typical of roasted Wuyi oolongs: clear orange to amber.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class: broad leaves, green-brown with darker, more oxidised edges.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting record exists for this tea alone. Expect what is typical of Wuyi rock teas: roast, mineral depth and some floral or fruit sweetness.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for Wuyi rock teas: a gaiwan, water near the boil and short steeps.

vintage_note: Little is documented about how this one is sold. As is usual for Wuyi rock teas, expect lots labelled by spring harvest year, often sold some months after roasting so the fire can settle.
description:
Jiu Long Pao, Nine Dragon Robe, is a name found on lists of Chinese oolongs and among the lesser-known Wuyi rock teas. Beyond that, little about it is documented in detail, so treat firm claims about its parentage with care.

The making is assumed from its class: Wuyi rock teas are shaken, partly oxidised and roasted, and the roast does much to shape the cup.

Expect the broad pattern of the class rather than a fixed flavour: roast first, then mineral weight and sweetness in later steeps. Brew it hot and short.

When buying, ask the seller for the harvest year, the roast level and where the leaf grew. A name alone tells you little here.
history: Little is documented about where and when this tea arose or who made it known. It appears by name in English-language lists of Chinese oolongs, but its history is not established in the material available.
